cards.front: Define hardware.
back: The physical components of a computer system.

cards.front: Which logic gate outputs 1 only when its two inputs are different?
back: XOR.

cards.front: Which CPU component performs calculations and logical comparisons?
back: Arithmetic logic unit (ALU).

cards.front: Which translator converts assembly language into machine code?
back: Assembler.

cards.front: Name the volatile main memory used for active programs and data.
back: RAM.

cards.front: What is an embedded system?
back: A computer built into a larger device to perform a dedicated or limited function.

cards.front: Explain the relationship between hardware and software.
back: Software supplies instructions and data that control operations.
Hardware provides the physical components that execute those instructions.

cards.front: Explain the difference between system software and application software.
back: System software manages computer resources and provides a platform.
Application software performs tasks for the end user.

cards.front: Give two functions of an operating system.
back: Any two of processor scheduling, memory management, device/I/O management, application management, file management or security.

cards.front: Explain the difference between machine code and assembly language.
back: Machine code is binary executed directly by a particular processor.
Assembly uses mnemonic instructions with a one-to-one correspondence to machine-code instructions.

cards.front: Explain the difference between volatile and non-volatile memory.
back: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed.
Non-volatile memory retains its contents without power.

cards.front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of cloud storage compared with local storage.
back: It can be accessed from different locations and can provide off-site backup.
It depends on connectivity/provider availability or may create privacy and ongoing-cost concerns.

cards.front: Give the outputs of AND, OR and XOR when A = 1 and B = 1.
back: AND = 1.
OR = 1.
XOR = 0.

cards.front: Describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
back: Fetch the next instruction from main memory into the CPU.
Decode it to determine the required operation.
Execute the instruction, including any required read or write.

cards.front: Explain how cache size can affect CPU performance.
back: Cache keeps useful instructions and data close to the CPU. A larger cache can reduce slower RAM accesses, but the benefit depends on the workload and does not guarantee a proportional speed increase.

cards.front: Compare RAM and ROM.
back: RAM is volatile and stores programs/data currently in use.
ROM is non-volatile and stores instructions or data that must persist.
Both provide electronic storage used by the computer system.

cards.front: Give three advantages of high-level languages over low-level languages.
back: They are easier for people to read and write.
Programs are faster to develop, test and maintain.
The source can usually be translated for different processor types.

cards.front: Explain why an SSD is suitable for a laptop.
back: It has no moving parts, so it is resistant to physical shock.
It provides fast access to programs and data.
It is quiet and generally uses less power than magnetic storage.

cards.front: Compare a compiler and an interpreter.
back: A compiler translates the whole high-level program and produces machine/object code.
The translated program can run later without translating every statement again.
An interpreter processes statements while the program runs and does not directly create a machine-code program.
Interpretation supports quick testing but requires the interpreter and may be slower during repeated execution.

cards.front: Explain the roles of the ALU, control unit, clock and registers.
back: The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations.
The control unit coordinates instruction processing and sends control signals.
The clock supplies timing signals that synchronise operations.
Registers hold immediate instructions, data or intermediate results inside the CPU.

cards.front: Compare magnetic and solid-state secondary storage.
back: An HDD stores magnetic patterns on rotating platters, using a moving read/write head. This gives mechanical delays, but often a low cost per gigabyte.

An SSD retains charge states in flash-memory cells and accesses data electronically. It has no moving parts and is usually faster and more resistant to knocks, but often costs more per gigabyte. Both need backups because either can fail.

cards.front: Explain how clock speed, cores and cache can affect CPU performance.
back: Higher clock speed allows more cycles each second.
Multiple cores can process more tasks simultaneously when software supports parallel work.
Larger cache reduces time spent waiting for main memory.
Overall improvement depends on the workload, software and other system bottlenecks.

cards.front: What is CPU cache?
back: A small amount of very fast, volatile memory built into or close to the CPU. It keeps copies of frequently or recently used instructions and data to reduce slower RAM accesses.

cards.front: If needed data is already in cache, why can the CPU use it sooner?
back: Accessing the cached copy is faster than retrieving it from RAM, so the CPU spends less time waiting.

cards.front: Does a larger cache preserve unsaved document changes when power is lost?
back: No. Cache is volatile, like RAM. The document must be saved to non-volatile storage.

cards.front: What does a clock speed of 3 GHz mean?
back: About 3 billion clock cycles per second. It does not mean every instruction takes exactly one cycle.

cards.front: Why might doubling CPU cores give little benefit to a particular program?
back: The program may rely on a sequential task that cannot use the extra cores. More available cores do not automatically divide every job.

cards.front: How does an operating system let several tasks make progress on one processor core?
back: It schedules processor time between tasks. Rapid switching can make the tasks appear to run at the same time.

cards.front: Why does a printer need a device driver?
back: The driver lets the operating system communicate with that particular device using the instructions it understands.

cards.front: What is the difference between a backup utility and an encryption utility?
back: Backup creates a recoverable copy. Encryption makes data unreadable without the appropriate key. Neither replaces the other.

cards.front: Is a compression tool application software just because the user opens it?
back: No. Its purpose is system maintenance or support, so it is a utility. Classification depends on its job, not who clicks it.

cards.front: How does a magnetic hard disk store binary data?
back: Patterns in magnetised regions on rotating platters represent data. A read/write head changes those patterns to write and detects them to read.

cards.front: Why does an HDD take time to reach a particular sector?
back: The head must move to the correct track and wait for the required sector to rotate underneath it.

cards.front: How does an SSD retain files without power?
back: Flash-memory cells retain electrical charge states that represent data. Reading and writing are electronic and do not require a moving head or platter.

cards.front: Why can magnetic tape be slower than an HDD for retrieving one specific file?
back: Tape must wind through intervening material to reach the location. An HDD can move directly to the relevant region, although it still has mechanical delays.

cards.front: Which storage technology do USB pen drives and SD memory cards use?
back: Solid-state flash storage. Their shapes and connections differ, but both retain data electronically without power.

cards.front: Why is synchronising a folder not necessarily a complete backup?
back: A deletion or unwanted change may synchronise too. Recovery depends on separately protected copies, version history and retention arrangements.

cards.front: Does cloud storage remove the need for physical storage devices?
back: No. Remote servers still use magnetic or solid-state devices. Cloud describes where the files are kept and accessed.

cards.front: For inputs A = 1 and B = 1, how do OR and XOR differ?
back: OR outputs 1 because at least one input is true. XOR outputs 0 because the two inputs are not different.

cards.front: How many rows are needed for every combination of three independent Boolean inputs?
back: Eight rows, because 2³ = 8. List each combination once before calculating intermediate outputs.

cards.front: Evaluate Q = (A AND B) OR NOT C for A = 0, B = 1 and C = 0.
back: A AND B is 0. NOT C is 1. Therefore Q is 0 OR 1, which is 1.

cards.front: Can a program compile successfully and still calculate the wrong answer?
back: Yes. A logic error can use valid syntax but the wrong calculation or condition. Testing is still needed after successful translation.

cards.front: Why does high-level source portability not guarantee that one executable runs on every processor?
back: The source can be translated for suitable systems, but compiled machine code is tied to a processor instruction set and its required runtime support.
